title: Fragmented IO: async scatter-load heuristics and hot-relink playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an engineering playbook and proposed heuristics for a fragmented/async model weight load flow that minimizes cold-start latency while enabling a low-risk hot-relink (hot-swap variant) for on-disk parameter replacement. The intent is pragmatic: avoid large synchronous mmap loads, tolerate partial residency, and provide an easy rollback path if a new weight fragment fails validation or causes regressions.

Background / motivation:
- We have recurring pain on cold starts for very large sharded models (>200GB) where full mmap/probe is expensive and spikes IO.
- Existing lazy-load proposals reduce initial latency but leave unclear failure modes for hot updates and for interop with KV cache priming.
- Customers using Dedicated/Private deployments sometimes need model binary patching (quantization overlays, quick tokenizer fixes) without downtime.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Reduce p50 cold-start generation latency for common short prompts by 20–40% via prioritized fragment streaming.
- Allow a safe, atomic on-disk relink of new parameter fragments with an observable fallback path (hot-relink).
- Keep per-host memory usage predictable; prevent cache thrash when many models share a node.
- Integrate with KV cache warmup: we want predictable priming behavior when backing weights are partially resident.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Files are stored as safetensors or safely-converted checkpoints; we assume index metadata is available quickly (small JSON per shard).
- Underlying OS is Linux; we rely on mmap/ madvise / posix_fadvise semantics for residency hints when available.
- Network fetch may be used for on-demand fragments (S3-like). We cannot assume microsecond fetches.

Key concepts / vocabulary used in this doc:
- fragment: contiguous range of parameters within a shard file that can be fetched/mapped independently (e.g., attention qkv block).
- residency score: runtime metric estimating how likely a fragment will be used soon (combines static topology, recent trace tokens).
- scatter-load: asynchronous parallel fetching/mmaping of prioritized fragments.
- hot-relink: an atomic on-disk swap procedure that repoints model instance(s) to a new fragment set without full service restarts.
- frozen-segment: read-only fragment mapped with checksum/validation gating before being used by kernels.

Design overview (high level):
1) quick-index stage (sub-50ms): load a small JSON index per model that lists fragment boundaries, sizes, affinitized kernels, and checksums. This index is tiny and allows the runtime to build a prioritized fragment queue.

2) priority queue & residency scoring:
   - Score = static_weight * (kernel_affinity) + runtime_weight * (trace_heatmap) + heuristics_factor.
   - Static weight: based on model architecture (e.g., embedding and first transformer block fragments get high static_weight).
   - Runtime heatmap: short-running token traces from recent requests on the same model version on the same node (sliding window).
   - Heuristic examples: num_heads, head_dim, known expensive layers (rope tables) get bumped.

3) scatter-load executor (async):
   - Top-K fragments are scheduled for parallel async fetch + mmap into an application-managed arena.
   - Each async op has a deadline relative to request SLO; if not available by decode time, fall back to on-demand soft-fetch (reads with smaller buffer) to avoid prolonged blocking.
   - Limit concurrent fetches per-model and per-host to reduce IO storms; use token-bucket to allow bursts when system is idle.

4) mmap + validation pipeline:
   - Map file regions read-only using MAP_SHARED, advise MADV_RANDOM for large fragments expected to be scanned; for cache-heavy fragments use MADV_WILLNEED only for the top-most prioritized items.
   - After mapping, compute a fast checksum (xxhash64) over a sampling of pages for integrity and to detect partial writes from upstream. If checksum mismatch, mark fragment invalid and trigger repair path.
   - Validation is done off the hot path: mapping succeeds, kernel usage must wait on fragment.ready flag. Low-latency fallbacks use smaller temp buffers to satisfy inference while validation proceeds.

5) hot-relink protocol (atomic on-disk flip):
   - A new version DAG for fragments is published to object store. Each fragment candidate includes: content file, checksum, size, and placement hints.
   - Staging: prefetch prioritized fragments to a staging area (local store path under /var/lib/rw/inference/staging/<model+ver>/) and validate checksums.
   - Coordinate with the model controller to ensure no in-flight writes: controller holds a per-model update lease (short TTL).
   - Step A - pin read-only handles: for instances that will remain on old version, the runtime keeps existing mmap handles open until safe to close.
   - Step B - create new symlink namespace: create a brand-new per-version directory and atomically swap the model root symlink (atomic rename of symlink target) so new instances open new files.
   - Step C - lazy activation: existing in-memory instances can opt-in to reconnect to new fragments by remapping incremental fragments when safe. This is not forced to avoid forcing GC on kernels.
   - Step D - fallback/rollback: if validation errors surface after relink, controller can move symlink back and signal instances to remap to the previous version. Instances should keep a small eviction-tolerant cache of previous fragments for a grace period.

6) kernel integration and partial-use semantics:
   - Kernels must tolerate partially-mapped parameters: they will check fragment.ready flag for each fragment they reference. If not ready, kernel either uses a local (temporary) small float buffer produced from lower-precision fallback or stalls briefly (configurable).
   - Provide two kernel policies: optimistic (prefer to proceed with fallback values) and conservative (stall until fragment.ready). Default per-model policy settable via model metadata.

7) KV cache priming interaction:
   - Prime heuristics detect that for certain workloads (few-shot chat) the KV access pattern is dominated by recent tokens; therefore we prioritize transformer tail fragments that service KV projection layers.
   - If KV cache is cold and fragment not present, schedule a low-priority prefetch for tail fragments when idle, but do not block generation. Telemetry should capture when priming would have avoided an on-demand fetch.

Telemetry and observability to collect:
- fragment_fetch_time_ms (histogram) per fragment class
- fragment_validation_latency_ms
- percent_fragments_present_at_infer_start (per-model)
- hot_relink_latency_ms and relink_success_rate
- kernel_fallback_count and fallback_type (precision-downgrade vs stall)

Failure modes and mitigation strategies:
- widespread IO storm: throttle scatter-load, rely on global token bucket, temporarily force conservative kernel policy to reduce memory churn.
- validation CRC mismatch after relink: auto-rollback and alert; keep old fragments pinned until at least N successful inference samples observed.
- partial network outage for shards: failover to remote-region mirror or attempt degraded-mode (small-probe-buffer decode) per policy.

Rollout plan (practical):
- Phase 0: feature gate behind runtime flag; enable on a single internal cluster with synthetic workloads (Dec 2025).
- Phase 1: shadow-mode on production traffic, collect telemetry, do not relink (Jan 2026).
- Phase 2: opt-in relink for non-critical models (canary customers), enable KV priming telemetry (Feb 2026).
- Phase 3: wide rollout with SLA guardrails and automated rollback (Mar 2026).

Operational checklist when performing a relink:
- ensure controller lease acquired (JIRA-INF-4319)
- prefetch top-10 prioritized fragments to staging and validate checksums
- run dry-run validation job that runs 100 synthetic short prompts and verifies latency/regression against baseline
- perform symlink flip during maintenance window or low-traffic target
- monitor kernel_fallback_count and fragment_fetch_time_ms closely for 15m post-flip

Open questions / TODOs:
- exact scoring coefficients for residency score; need offline experiments across weight layouts and real traces (Marco to own).
- optimal page sampling rate for fast checksum; tradeoff between detection quality and CPU cost.
- fallback buffer sizing strategy: how big should temp on-demand buffers be before we prefer to stall?
- interaction with cloud volume snapshotting semantics (some clouds do copy-on-write behavior on symlinked files) - legal/infra consult needed.

Notes to reviewers:
- This tries to balance safety with aggressive latency wins. It intentionally favors a staged, observable relink rather than a blind in-place overwrite.
- The method should integrate cleanly with our existing weight residency controller and parameter residency metrics. See linked PR for prototype implementation.

Appendix: quick example sequence (happy path):
1) model instance receives request, loads small JSON index, computes top-K (k=6) fragments: embedding frag, first-attn-qkv frag, first-ffn frag, tail-attn frag x3.
2) schedules scatter-load of those 6 fragments; 4 land before decode; 2 don't and a tiny fallback buffer holds placeholders.
3) decode proceeds with minimal stall; KV cache primes tail fragments after answer and warms fragment heatmap for next request.
4) later operator triggers hot-relink to apply quantized overlay; staging prefetch validates checksums; controller flips symlink; new instances open new files; old instances gradually remap when safe.
